title: Reading Samuel

objectives.can: Read the prose of Samuel: longer scenes, quick dialogue and some hard text.

explanation.summary: The books of Samuel tell the rise of Samuel, Saul and David in long, patient scenes. This lesson reads 1 Samuel 3:1–10, the night call of Samuel, and says what to look for in Samuel's prose: setting clauses, repeated calls and answers, and a few places where the Hebrew is hard.

sections.heading: What you will meet in Samuel
body: Samuel's narrative is slower than the Genesis narrative. A scene begins with several clauses that set the stage, and then the events begin. Dialogue is quick and often in very short sentences, and the same few words go back and forth between the speakers. The story is long, so a reader has to keep track of people, places and what each one knows.

The passage for this lesson is 1 Samuel 3:1–10. The rest of the chapter is 3:11–21, where the LORD tells Samuel what will happen to Eli's house and Samuel tells Eli in the morning. In 3:13 the ancient versions differ from the Hebrew text, and this is one of several places in the book where scholars compare the Hebrew with the Greek version and with the scrolls found at Qumran. We shall read the Hebrew as it stands.

sections.heading: Setting the scene
body: The first verses of the chapter are not a chain of events. They are a description. In 3:1 two clauses begin with a subject and give the situation: וְהַנַּעַר שְׁמוּאֵל מְשָׁרֵת, with the participle מְשָׁרֵת for 'serving', and וּדְבַר יְהוָה הָיָה יָקָר, with a qatal and an adjective. A clause with אֵין, אֵין חָזוֹן נִפְרָץ, says that a vision was not widespread. These clauses give the background of the story, the way a stage is set before the actors move.

A frame with וַיְהִי often follows and marks the start of the action. In 3:2 וַיְהִי בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא, 'and it was on that day', begins the scene proper, and again the next words are participles: Eli is שֹׁכֵב, lying, and his eyes are failing. In 3:3 the lamp is not yet out and Samuel is lying down, וּשְׁמוּאֵל שֹׁכֵב. The participle means that the person was in that state when the event came.

The little word טֶרֶם, 'not yet', stands in the same kind of clause. In 3:3 it is followed by a yiqtol, טֶרֶם יִכְבֶּה, 'the lamp had not yet gone out'; in 3:7 by a qatal, טֶרֶם יָדַע, and then by a yiqtol, טֶרֶם יִגָּלֶה. The Hebrew does not distinguish 'had' and 'was' as English does; the context fixes the time as past.

sections.heading: Calls and answers
body: The heart of the scene is three calls. The LORD calls, Samuel runs to Eli with the words הִנְנִי כִּי קָרָאתָ לִי, 'here I am, for you called me', and Eli answers לֹא קָרָאתִי and sends him back, with the imperatives שׁוּב and שְׁכָב. The same sentences return in 3:5, 3:6 and 3:8, with only small changes: in 3:6 Eli adds בְנִי, 'my son', and in 3:8 the narrator reports that Eli understood.

To say that the LORD called again, 3:6 uses וַיֹּסֶף יְהוָה קְרֹא, literally 'the LORD added to call'. This is an idiom: a form of יָסַף followed by an infinitive says that someone does a thing again. The infinitive here is קְרֹא, the construct infinitive of קָרָא. The same idiom appears in 3:8 with the words בַּשְּׁלִשִׁית, 'the third time'.

Eli's instruction in 3:9 is a small speech with its own order. After the imperatives לֵךְ שְׁכָב comes וְהָיָה אִם יִקְרָא אֵלֶיךָ, 'and it will be, if he calls to you', and then the weqatal וְאָמַרְתָּ introduces what Samuel is to say: דַּבֵּר יְהוָה כִּי שֹׁמֵעַ עַבְדֶּךָ. The speech Samuel is told to give begins after the weqatal and ends with עַבְדֶּךָ. When he actually answers in 3:10 he says דַּבֵּר כִּי שֹׁמֵעַ עַבְדֶּךָ, and the name is not there.

sections.heading: Infinitive absolutes and oaths
body: Samuel is rich in two features that do not occur in 3:1–10 but will meet you everywhere else in the book. The first is the infinitive absolute, a form of the verb used beside a finite verb of the same root for emphasis. In 1 Samuel 2:30 the LORD's words begin אָמוֹר אָמַרְתִּי, 'I surely said', with the infinitive absolute first; in 14:39 the same pattern is מוֹת יָמוּת, 'he shall surely die'.

The second is the oath formula. 1 Samuel 14:39 begins כִּי חַי יְהוָה, 'for as the LORD lives', and the verb that follows is what the speaker swears. In 19:6 Saul swears חַי יְהוָה אִם יוּמָת. After an oath, אִם introduces what will not happen, so the words say that David will not be put to death. This use of אִם is a feature of oaths, and it is not the word for 'if' in a condition.

sections.heading: Hard places
body: Even in a famous scene there are words that are not easy. In 3:1 the participle נִפְרָץ is a form of פָּרַץ, whose dictionary sense is 'break through'. Here it is usually taken to mean that a vision was 'widespread' or 'frequent', and commentators and translators disagree about the exact word. In 3:2 the verb הֵחֵלּוּ is a Hiphil of חָלַל, a root whose Qal and Piel mean 'defile' or 'profane'; in the Hiphil it normally means 'begin', and the clause says that his eyes had begun to grow dim.

The ancient versions of Samuel often differ from the Hebrew, and in some chapters, 3:13 among them, the difference changes the sense. A learner does not need to settle such matters. It is enough to notice that the Hebrew is sometimes uncertain and to read it as it stands, with the question in mind.

sections.heading: How to read the passage
body: Read 3:1–10 once for the story. Then go through it again. Mark the participles and the clauses that set the scene, mark each of the three calls and the answers, and mark where each speech begins and ends. When you meet a word you do not know, try the sentence without it first.

misunderstandings: Reading a participle clause such as וְעֵלִי שֹׁכֵב as the next event. It describes the situation in which the event takes place.
Reading וַיֹּסֶף as 'and he added' with nothing added. With an infinitive it means to do something again.
Taking אִם after an oath as 'if'. After an oath formula it introduces what will not happen.
Thinking that every uncertain word needs a correction. The Hebrew of Samuel is read as it stands, and where witnesses differ the difference is noted, not decided by the reader.

deeper.heading: Samuel and its textual witnesses
body: The text of Samuel is less smooth than that of most books. Scrolls from Qumran sometimes agree with the Greek translation against the Hebrew text as it was handed down, and sometimes with the handed-down text. Editors weigh the evidence passage by passage. A reading course keeps to the handed-down text and notes the questions.

examples.analysis: A verse that sets the stage and has no event. The participle מְשָׁרֵת says that the boy Samuel was serving, the qatal הָיָה with the adjective יָקָר says the word was rare, and the clause with אֵין and the Niphal participle נִפְרָץ says that vision was not widespread.

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: And the LORD called yet again Samuel. And Samuel arose and went to Eli, and said: 'Here am I; for thou didst call me.' And he answered: 'I called not, my son; lie down again.'

examples.analysis: וַיֹּסֶף with the infinitive קְרֹא means 'again': the LORD called again. Then two wayyiqtol verbs, וַיָּקָם and וַיֵּלֶךְ, take Samuel to Eli. Eli's answer ends with the two imperatives שׁוּב and שְׁכָב and the address בְנִי.

examples.analysis: טֶרֶם is 'not yet'. It stands before a qatal (יָדַע) and again before a yiqtol (יִגָּלֶה, a Niphal). The clauses give the background to the three calls: Samuel did not yet know the LORD.

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: Therefore Eli said unto Samuel: 'Go, lie down; and it shall be, if thou be called, that thou shalt say: Speak, LORD; for Thy servant heareth.' So Samuel went and lay down in his place.

examples.analysis: Eli's instruction. Imperatives (לֵךְ, שְׁכָב), then וְהָיָה and a conditional with אִם and the yiqtol יִקְרָא. The weqatal וְאָמַרְתָּ gives what Samuel is to say next: the imperative דַּבֵּר, the participle שֹׁמֵעַ, and the noun עַבְדֶּךָ with the suffix 'your'.

quoted.english: For, as the LORD liveth, who saveth Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die.' But there was not a man among all the people that answered him.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It turns the verb into a noun
It makes the verb emphatic: he shall surely die
It makes the verb a question
check.explain: An infinitive absolute of the same root beside a finite verb strengthens it. The sentence follows an oath, so the speaker is swearing that it will happen.

check.prompt: What does Saul swear with חַי יְהוָה אִם יוּמָת?

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: And Saul hearkened unto the voice of Jonathan; and Saul swore: 'As the LORD liveth, he shall not be put to death.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: That David will not be put to death
That David will certainly be put to death
That he will ask whether David should die
check.explain: חַי יְהוָה is the oath formula, 'as the LORD lives'. After an oath, אִם introduces what will not happen. The verb יוּמָת is a Hophal, 'he will be put to death'.

reading.why: A full scene of Samuel's prose: setting clauses with participles and טֶרֶם, three calls repeated with small changes, short quick dialogue, an instruction with imperatives, a conditional and a weqatal, and an idiom with יָסַף.
